overview: A buck converter steps a higher DC voltage down to a lower one efficiently, switching power on and off rapidly rather than burning off the difference as heat the way a simple linear regulator does — meaning it stays cool even when dropping something like 12V down to 5V at real current, where a linear regulator would waste a lot of energy as heat. This module exposes a small trimpot to adjust the output voltage to whatever's needed, which is also its most common trap for beginners: it ships set to some arbitrary voltage, not necessarily what your project needs, and must be measured and adjusted with a multimeter before connecting anything voltage-sensitive.
simpleSummary: A small module that safely steps a higher voltage down to a lower one, like 12V down to 5V.

specifications.efficiency: ~85-95%, far better than a linear regulator dropping the same voltage difference

pinMap.name: IN+
pinMap.currentLimit: Depends on output load and efficiency

pinMap.name: OUT+
pinMap.function: Regulated positive output — voltage set by the onboard trimpot.
pinMap.gotcha: Ships set to an arbitrary voltage from the factory — always measure and adjust with a multimeter under no load before connecting anything voltage-sensitive.

pinMap.name: OUT-
pinMap.function: Output ground, shares a common reference with input ground.

useCases.title: Battery-to-logic voltage step-down
useCases.scenario: Step a 12V battery pack down to a clean 5V for powering a microcontroller and sensors.

useCases.title: Multi-voltage project power distribution
useCases.scenario: Generate several different regulated voltages from one higher-voltage supply for mixed-voltage components.

oftenConfusedWith: Boost converter (steps voltage up, not down)
7805/AMS1117 linear regulator (simpler, less efficient, more heat)
oftenUpgradedTo: Higher-current buck modules for power-hungry loads like LED strips or multiple servos
